extracted.intended_audience: educated British public and politically engaged readers (late 18th-century pamphlet/political audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A political-constitutional pamphlet arguing for the legal and practical primacy of hereditary succession and against doctrines of popular election, cashiering governors, or forming a new government. It explains historical statutes, principles, and practical consequences to rebut a faction (the 'Revolution Society').

rubrics_metrics.name: King's legitimacy rests on hereditary succession, not popular election
rubrics_metrics.description: The crown of Great Britain is held by a fixed rule of succession; the king does not owe his crown to the choice of his people and is therefore a lawful sovereign irrespective of popular election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument cites the present practice and law that the monarch succeeds by inheritance; warns that treating election as necessary would make the British king no better than 'usurpers' elsewhere. Examples: heirs and successors will come to the crown 'with the same contempt of their choice' as the present king.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of Right (1688) contains no right to elect governors
rubrics_metrics.description: If the principles of the Revolution are anywhere found, they are in the Declaration of Right, which contains no language asserting a general right 'to choose our own governors, to cashier them for misconduct, and to form a government for ourselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the precise statutory text (the act of 1 William & Mary, sess. 2, ch. 2) as the authoritative source; do not import the Revolution Society's asserted rights into constitutional principle when they are absent from the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights and succession are declared together and bound indissolubly
rubrics_metrics.description: The Declaration of Right declares 'the rights and liberties of the subject, and for settling the succession of the crown' as one body, indissolubly connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations of the Revolution must respect that Parliament tied individual rights to a settled line of succession; one should not separate an asserted popular right to choose from the statutory settlement of succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later settlement (12th & 13th William) entrenched hereditary Protestant succession for stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of the 12th and 13th of King William further limited the crown to the Protestant line, expressly linking certainty in succession to the 'peace, quiet, and security of the realm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat statutory limitations (e.g., naming the Electress Sophia and her Protestant heirs) as intentional constitutional policy to preserve unity and avoid the perils of elective monarchy; this is factual legislative intent used to rebut claims for popular election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-case deviations cannot establish general constitutional principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A temporary or special-case law made for an individual (e.g., the Revolution's departure in favor of William) does not justify deriving a general principle like elective monarchy; 'privilegium non transit in exemplum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extrapolate from cases of necessity to broad rules; legal principles should not be founded on isolated expedients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession secures continuity of law and liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: An hereditary crown is presented as the best guarantee for perpetuating and preserving liberties and for maintaining continuity of statute law and constitutional order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that invalidating hereditary legitimacy would cast doubt on the validity of long-standing statutes (Habeas Corpus, Petition of Right, etc.) enacted under prior lawful sovereigns; treat continuity as a core value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cashiering governors for 'misconduct' is an unsafe, imprecise remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of a public right to 'cashier' governors for misconduct is too loose and indefinite to sustain stable government; the Revolution grounds its acts on grave, specific charges (e.g., subversion of Church and State), not on vague misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor institutional safeguards (frequent Parliaments, impeachment, ministers' responsibility) over a general right of deposition; recognize that forcible removal is often extra-legal and tantamount to war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary change should conserve and repair, not decompose the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: When constitutional change is necessary, it should regenerate only the deficient part and preserve the rest of the ancient constitution; avoid decomposing the whole civil order to create a new state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize conservative repair: altered parts should be fitted to the unaltered organs, ensuring continuity rather than wholesale innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of moral competence constrain what bodies may renounce
rubrics_metrics.description: Even supreme powers have moral limits: constituent parts (House of Lords, Commons) are not morally competent to dissolve fundamental institutions or to abdicate permanent constitutional functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction between abstract sovereign competence and moral/constitutional competence to argue that some acts (e.g., dissolving the Commons) would be illegitimate even if technically possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective-monarchy doctrine undermines positive law and historic statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: If no throne is lawful but the elective, then past acts and laws passed under prior monarchs risk invalidation and the legal order becomes unstable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to concrete statutory consequences as a reductio ad absurdum of the elective doctrine: historic statutes and legal innovations depend on continuity of lawful sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric of calling the king 'servant of the people' mischaracterizes constitutional role
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling the sovereign 'servant of the people' confuses legal reality with rhetorical flattery; the law designates the monarch 'our sovereign lord the king,' and the people obey the law in him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject emotive or novel styles of address as inadequate substitutes for constitutional distinctions; avoid conflating moral service with legal subordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment and parliamentary oversight are preferable safeguards to popular deposal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution's constitutional machinery (frequent parliaments, impeachment, ministerial responsibility) provides superior protection against abuses than crude claims of election or cashiering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate institutional mechanisms for accountability rather than popular or extra-legal remedies; cite statutory provisions (e.g., no pardon under great seal pleadable to impeachment) as concrete protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: The popular 'rights' claimed by factional societies do not represent the general body of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'new bill of rights' advanced by the Revolution Society is claimed to belong to that faction alone; the body of the people disclaim it and will resist its practical assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame such doctrines as sectarian or factional (e.g., 'these gentlemen of the Old Jewry') and argue that widespread public sentiment and law oppose radical reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions are extraordinary remedies, to be judged by grave necessity and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Dethroning a sovereign is essentially a question of war and extraordinary statecraft; it is not a routine constitutional procedure and must be reserved for overwhelming necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat revolution as last resort; decisions are to be made by those capable of weighing dispositions, means, and probable consequences rather than by common or speculative minds.
